rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: Most place al-Mulk in the middle Makkan period, though its revelation date is not definitively established.
rows.anchor: was revealed, most consider it to be from the middle of the Makkan period.

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Sayings attributed to the Prophet call the surah Tabārak or by its opening words, Blessed Is He in Whose Hand Lies Sovereignty.
rows.anchor: In the sayings attributed to the Prophet, it is called by the first word, Tabārak, meaning “Blessed,” or by the first few words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith calls the surah a shield or protector from punishment in the grave.
rows.anchor: Sūrat Tabārak is a shield ( māniʿ) from the punishment of the grave.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some call the surah al-Munjiyyah, the Savior, after a report that its thirty verses intercede for its reciter until forgiven.
rows.anchor: a sūrah in the Quran which contains thirty verses that will intercede on behalf of one who recites it until he is forgiven

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another hadith says the surah's thirty verses argue for its companion until bringing him into the Garden.
rows.anchor: thirty verses that will argue on behalf of its companion until it causes him to enter the Garden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadiths and Companion sayings underpin the belief that reciting the surah spares a person trials in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: one who recites this sūrah will be spared from trials in both this life and the next.

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to have wished the surah would be in every member of his community's heart.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said regarding al-Mulk,“I would love for it to be in the heart of every person among my community”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mulk is among the Quran's best-known and most frequently recited surahs.
rows.anchor: known and most frequently recited

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening establishes God's omnipotence and creation's perfection in verses 1–4, then says jinn cannot penetrate the heavens in verse 5.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with an attestation to God’s omnipotence and the perfection of creation (vv. 1–4), followed by an assertion of the inability of the jinn to penetrate the heavens (v. 5).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–12 contrast the dreadful end of those denying God's messengers with the end of those who fear God.
rows.anchor: The dreadful ends of those who deny God’s messengers (vv. 6–11) are contrasted with the final ends of those who fear God (v. 12).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 13–24 reassert divine omnipotence and omniscience through interposed statements and rhetorical questions.
rows.anchor: God’s omnipotence and omniscience is then reasserted through a series of interposed statements and rhetorical questions (vv. 13–24)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah concludes with questions the Prophet is told to ask those who question him about the end of time.
rows.anchor: the sūrah concludes with a series of questions that the Prophet is told to pose to those who question him regarding the end of time (vv. 25–30).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven heavens may mean the heavens alone, the whole created order, or universal levels of existence used in hierarchical cosmologies.
rows.anchor: The heavens can be seen as a reference only to the heavens, the whole of the created order, or the universal levels or grades of existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentaries use the heavens as levels or grades that ground hierarchical cosmological schemes.
rows.anchor: the last of which serves as a basis for various hierarchical cosmological schemes in some commentaries.

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Tafāwut means lack of proportion or balance in which parts fail to connect with one another.
rows.anchor: Disproportion translates tafāwut, which here indicates something that lacks proportion or balance such that parts of it fail to connect with other parts of it (R, Z)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some equate the absence of disproportion with the absence of rifts, as in the description of the sky in 50:6.
rows.anchor: thus some say it has the same meaning as rifts in 50:6

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may mean either no rifts between the seven heavens or, more generally, no gaps in God's creation.
rows.anchor: The lack of disproportion can be understood as the absence of rifts between the seven heavens or more generally as an indication that there are no gaps in God’s creation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that all things are created in truth is supported by 44:38–39 and linked to several other verses on creation.
rows.anchor: As several verses indicate, all things are created in truth, as in 44:38–39

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The returning eye may be humbled because an eye seeking defects comes back humiliated or debased.
rows.anchor: That the eye returns humbled could also mean that an eye that tries to find defect returns “humiliated” or “debased” (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse relates to 4:82, which says that contemplation of the Quran finds no discrepancy in it.
rows.anchor: This verse is also related to 4:82, which maintains that for one who contemplates the Quran no discrepancy will be found in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's opening recalls Noah's statement that God made the earth open and its paths spacious, and is linked to 20:53, 21:31, and 43:10.
rows.anchor: The beginning of this verse is similar to part of what Noah says to his people in 71:19–20

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran often commands travel on earth so people will reflect on creation.
rows.anchor: The command to travel or journey upon the earth and reflect upon the nature of the created order is a frequent refrain in the Quran.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Travel is usually connected with life's transience, with examples across the Quran.
rows.anchor: It is usually mentioned in relation to the transience of life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Travel can also prompt understanding of God's creative power, as in the command to observe creation's origin and next genesis in 29:20.
rows.anchor: but is also mentioned in relation to understanding the nature of God’s creative power, as in 29:20

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The travel exhortation calls for reflection that opens the heart to truth; 22:46 says hearts, not eyes, can go blind.
rows.anchor: The exhortation to travel or journey is thus an exhortation to reflect and contemplate, so that the heart may open to the truth, as in 22:46

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse parallels 16:79, where God alone holds the birds in midair and this is a sign for believers.
rows.anchor: Cf. 16:79: Have they not considered the birds, made subservient, in midair? None holds them save God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says that trust in God deserving of Him would bring provision like the birds, which leave hungry and return full.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states, “Were you to trust in God as He merits, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds; they depart with empty stomachs and return full”

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: The face-down walker is a metaphor for disbelievers who ignore the path around them and fail to consider their real condition, absorbed in petty and immediate desires.
rows.anchor: One who walks with his face stooped down is seen as a metaphor for disbelievers, who do not look at the path ahead, to the right, or to the left in this life (Q, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image is also read as referring to disbelievers gathered face-down for Hell in 25:34.
rows.anchor: It is also seen as a reference to the state of disbelievers in the Hereafter; as 25:34 says

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers walk upright, seeing the way and avoiding afflictions that could lead them astray.
rows.anchor: In contrast, believers are said to walk upright, so that they see and are not beset by afflictions that would cause them to go astray.

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the oath-monger verses with al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, a Quraysh leader and determined opponent of the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Mughīrah, a leader among the Quraysh and one of the Prophet’s staunchest opponents (Z).

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others take the target to be the Prophet's detractors generally, including Abū Jahl, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Yahūth, and al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq.
rows.anchor: Others propose that it may refer to his detractors in general, such as Abū Jahl, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Yahūth, and al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq (Z).

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: A vile oath-monger may be someone who frequently swears falsely.
rows.anchor: Vile oath-monger refers to one given to frequent swearing by falsehood (JJ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may mean someone who swears falsely by God's name.
rows.anchor: or one who swears falsely by God’s Name (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even pre-Islamic Arabia regarded excessive oath-taking as a vice; the Quran's position is discussed at 5:89.
rows.anchor: Even in pre-Islamic Arabia it was considered a vice to be immoderate in taking oaths.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: A slanderer spreads gossip to create discord and turn people against one another.
rows.anchor: one who spreads gossip in order to create discord and turn people against one another (Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadiths say those who spread calumny or gossip will not enter Paradise; the source links this vice with backbiting at 49:12.
rows.anchor: which can also mean “gossip,” will not enter Paradise (IK)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: A hinderer of good can be a miser who encourages miserliness or someone who blocks the way to Islam.
rows.anchor: Hinderer of good refers either to one who is miserly and encourages miserliness or to one who bars the way to Islam (Z).

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Zanīm denotes someone born illegitimately.
rows.anchor: Ignoble translates zanīm, which indicates one who is born illegitimately (Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zanīm may instead relate to zanamah, the fleshy skin below a goat's ears, and thus mean something with no positive function.
rows.anchor: It may also be related to the word zanamah, which denotes the fleshy skin hanging below the ears of a goat.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children should not outweigh qualities of the heart, since on Judgment Day neither avails except for one who comes with a sound heart; the theme appears in many verses.
rows.anchor: This verse alludes to the Quranic teaching that one should not put stock in worldly wealth and outward appearances, but in those things that reflect the nature of the heart

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, verses 14–15 ask whether his wealth and children cause him to dismiss God's signs as ancient fables.
rows.anchor: Alternately, vv. 14–15 can be read, “Is it because he possesses wealth and children that when Our signs are read to him he says, ‘Fables of those of old’?”(JJ, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling revelation ancient fables was a common disbeliever's dismissal, also found in 83:13 and eight other verses.
rows.anchor: Referring to the Prophet’s revelations as fables of those of old was a common way for the disbelievers to dismiss the message

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators read branding the snout idiomatically as marking someone with indelible disgrace.
rows.anchor: Most commentators take this to be an idiomatic expression meaning,“We will stigmatize him with indelible disgrace” (Iṣ).

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say the promise came true when al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah's nose was cut off at Badr.
rows.anchor: Some believe that this promise was fulfilled when al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah’s nose was cut off at the Battle of Badr (JJ).

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: The brand may reveal his true nature so he cannot conceal it, which accords with the guilty being known by their marks in 55:41.
rows.anchor: It could also mean that God will make his true nature apparent to all, so that he cannot hide it

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The translation reads bi as about rather than for: someone asks the Prophet who will be punished and when.
rows.anchor: The translation of v. 1 is based upon reading the preposition bi to mean about rather than “for,”

rows.speaker: Many commentators
rows.claim: Many instead read that a supplicant asked for punishment, paralleling 22:47 and the request attributed to Nadr ibn al-Ḥārith in 8:32.
rows.anchor: Many commentators, however, read the verse “a supplicator supplicated for” or “a petitioner petitioned for.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nadr sought to hasten punishment, unknowingly supplicated against himself, and received the punishment when killed in captivity at Badr in 2/624.
rows.anchor: Nadr ibn al-Ḥārith is believed to have supplicated against himself and to have unknowingly requested the punishment he received at the Battle of Badr (2/624), when he was killed in captivity (W, Z).

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say the verse was revealed in response to the Quraysh adversary Abū Jahl.
rows.anchor: According to others, the verse was revealed in response to another of the Prophet’s adversaries among the Quraysh, Abū Jahl (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source connects requests to hasten punishment with several Quranic passages.
rows.anchor: regarding those who seek to hasten the punishment, see 10:50–51; 16:1; 26:204–7; 29:53–54; 34:30; 37:176–77; 42:18; 51:14, 59.

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the Spirit as Gabriel, the Trustworthy Spirit mentioned at 26:193.
rows.anchor: Most commentators interpret the Spirit as a reference to the Archangel Gabriel (IK, Q, Ṭ), who is referred to as the Trustworthy Spirit in 26:193.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The Spirit may instead be another angel.
rows.anchor: It may also refer to another angel

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The Spirit may refer to a dead person's spirit as it leaves the body.
rows.anchor: or to the spirit of a dead person when the spirit is taken from the body (Q)

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: The fifty-thousand-year day is the Resurrection Day, whose duration applies to disbelievers.
rows.anchor: A day whose measure is fifty thousand years is understood to be the Day of Resurrection, which will be as fifty thousand years for the disbelievers (IK, Q).

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says God will lighten the Resurrection Day for a believer until it feels shorter than performing an obligatory prayer in worldly life.
rows.anchor: When asked about the length of the Day of Resurrection, the Prophet is reported to have said

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Others interpret fifty thousand as the distance between Heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: Others say that fifty thousand refers to the distance between Heaven and earth (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The difference between time in the Divine or spiritual realm and worldly time is also indicated at 22:47, 32:5, and 97:3.
rows.anchor: The disparity between time in the Divine or spiritual realm and time in this world is indicated in several places in the Quran

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Although the preceding verses clearly concern jinn, this verse may address jinn.
rows.anchor: Although the preceding verses clearly refer to the jinn, this verse can be seen as a reference to either the jinn (R)

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: Alternatively, the verse may address the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: or the Quraysh (Bg).

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators connect the verse to a seven-year drought that would end if disbelievers accepted Muhammad as God's messenger.
rows.anchor: According to many commentators, this verse refers to a seven-year drought that would be relieved, were the disbelievers to accept Muhammad as a messenger of God (Bg).

rows.speaker: Bg, IK, Q, R
rows.claim: Abundant water may allude to divine provision, rizq.
rows.anchor: Abundant water can be seen as an allusion to Divine Provision ( rizq; Bg, IK, Q, R)

rows.speaker: Bg, R
rows.claim: Abundant water may signify all manner of benefit and good.
rows.anchor: all manner of benefit and good, (Bg, R)

rows.speaker: Bg, Ṭ
rows.claim: Abundant water may signify an easy and abundant life.
rows.anchor: a life of ease and abundance (Bg,Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Abundant water may refer to Paradise, often described with gardens and flowing rivers.
rows.anchor: or Paradise, which is often described as having Gardens with rivers running below

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Conversely, it can mean provision by which God lets the astray deceive themselves and go further astray gradually.
rows.anchor: Conversely, this verse can be understood as a reference to the wealth and provision by which God allows those who are astray to continue fooling themselves, going further astray “little by little” (cf. 7:182; 68:44; Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The verses generally describe those who failed to follow God's Commands.
rows.anchor: In general these verses are understood to indicate those who failed to follow the Commands of God (Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: one Shiite interpretation
rows.claim: A Shiite reading takes verse 43 to mean they were not followers of the Imams, alluding to failure to follow Shiite leaders.
rows.anchor: But one Shiite interpretation of v. 43 would be, “and we were not among the followers of the leaders (aʾimmah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally says they plunged with those who plunged.
rows.anchor: Literally, this verse reads “and we plunged with those who plunged.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Quranic usage, khāḍa implies plunging into discourse or vanity and falsehood, as in several other verses.
rows.anchor: However, as employed in the Quran the verb khāḍa (“to plunge”) implies khāḍa fi’l-ḥadīth (“plunged into discourse”) or khāḍa fi’l-bāṭil (“plunged into vanity or falsehood”);

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The verse may mean they participated in worldly vanities and went astray.
rows.anchor: This verse thus indicates that they partook of the vanities of this world and went astray (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Alternatively, they associated with those whom God cursed for calling the Prophet a sorcerer.
rows.anchor: it could also mean that they associated with those whom God cursed for calling the Prophet a sorcerer (Q).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some understand they as disbelievers, as in 36:65 where their mouths are sealed.
rows.anchor: Here they is understood by some as a reference to the disbelievers (Q), as in 36:65

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Others understand they to mean all created beings.
rows.anchor: Others say they refers to all created beings (R).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some say the verse means that on the Day, no soul can speak except by God's leave, as 11:105 states.
rows.anchor: Some say this verse does not indicate speech as such, but that on the Day it comes, no soul shall speak, save by His Leave (11:105; Q).
